item.title: How to work from home?
item.description: Have a sense of urgency. Get a dedicated place. No distractions. Work 8 hours a day. No more. No less. Work as the very first thing of the day.

item.title: How to code review?
item.description: Consider not making code review approval mandatory. When people can deploy, they own it. When people own it, they care for it. You should comment.

item.title: How to interview?
item.description: First, ask if it’s still a good time for the candidate to do the interview. It’s rare, but they might not be in a good place.

item.title: How to write tech doc?
item.description: Use simple words. Write small sentences. Don’t use acronyms.

item.title: How to write a git commit message?
item.description: Limit the subject line to 50 chars. Write like you’re giving orders. Start with a verb. One line often suffices. Limit the body lines to 72 chars.

item.title: How to learn a new language?
item.description: Caveat This below doesn’t apply if you are new at programming. If you are, pick a language and build small things first.

item.title: How to estimate?
item.description: Don’t spend too much time on estimates. Perfect estimates don’t exist. They are guesses. “Man makes plans, God laughs.” But estimates still matter.

item.title: How to test code?
item.description: Remember that you have to maintain tests. Keep code simple. Keep tests simpler. Avoid abstractions in code. Ban them in tests.

item.title: How to debug anything?
item.description: Be great at debugging. Read the error messages. Start from the last message. Hidden in the noise, you may find the solution. Stay calm.
